term: Energy and water use of AI
oneSentence: These terms describe the electricity, water and related emissions linked to building and running AI systems, and the choices that can reduce those impacts.
plainExplanation:
AI systems rely on physical infrastructure: chips, servers, data centres, networks and cooling equipment. Training a model and using it later both require electricity. Some facilities also use water, often for cooling. That means AI has resource use and environmental effects beyond the screen.

These related terms are not identical. Energy and water use of AI refers to direct resource consumption. Carbon footprint of AI refers to greenhouse gas emissions linked to that energy use and the wider lifecycle. Environmental footprint is broader still: it can include emissions, water, materials, electronic waste and land use. Sustainability asks whether the system can meet its purpose while keeping those impacts, costs and trade-offs manageable over time.

What goes in? Requests from users, data moved across networks, and computing work on processors such as GPUs. What happens? Machines perform calculations, generate heat, and cooling systems remove that heat. What comes out? Useful results, but also electricity demand, possible water consumption, emissions that depend on the local power mix, and hardware wear over time.

The amount varies a lot. A small model used efficiently may have a modest footprint. A larger model, frequent use, repeated retries, or hosting in a region with carbon-intensive electricity can raise it. This is why people often compare model size, hardware type, deployment choice and how many outputs are really needed.

These terms are often confused with compute. Compute means the amount of processing work. It helps explain resource use, but it is not the same thing. Two systems can use similar compute yet have different emissions or water use because location, hardware efficiency, cooling method and electricity source differ.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting paper forms in an office
everydayAnalogy.story: Imagine a team in Arusha, Bogotá and Vienna helping group survey forms that raise the same issue. If they print every form, keep the lights on late, and run extra fans because the room gets hot, the job uses more electricity and materials. If they also bring in water for cooling because the room overheats, resource use rises further. The useful output is the grouped list of issues, but the office still used power, water and supplies to produce it. A better process, such as sorting only the needed pages and using a cooler room, can reduce the impact without changing the goal.

mapping.aiElement: Processors doing repeated calculations for training or inference

mapping.analogyElement: Lights, fans and a hot room
mapping.aiElement: Electricity use and heat generated by computing equipment

mapping.analogyElement: Water brought in to cool the room
mapping.aiElement: Water used directly or indirectly in cooling data-centre operations
The AI system's output or service delivered to users

everydayAnalogy.limitation: An office team is slow and visible, while AI runs in data centres and networks that users do not see directly. Also, AI impacts depend heavily on hardware efficiency, electricity source, cooling design and model architecture, which have no close match in the paper-sorting story. The analogy helps show that useful outputs still require physical resources, but it does not measure those impacts accurately.

visual.title: From AI request to environmental footprint
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain how an AI task leads to electricity use, heat, cooling needs, and broader environmental impacts, and why carbon footprint is only one part of the picture.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with five boxes. Start with an AI task, then computing hardware, then heat and cooling, then resource use, then broader impacts. Read the arrows as cause and effect: each stage creates the conditions for the next, and different design choices can reduce or increase the final footprint.

steps.label: AI task
steps.explanation: A model is trained or asked to generate an output. More tasks, larger models or repeated retries usually mean more processing work.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rounded rectangle labelled 'AI task' with small icons for training and answering a prompt.

steps.label: Hardware runs
steps.explanation: Chips and servers carry out calculations. This stage uses electricity and depends on hardware efficiency.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a server-and-chip box connected by an arrow from 'AI task'. Add a small meter icon labelled 'electricity'.

steps.label: Heat builds up
steps.explanation: Computing creates heat. As workload rises, cooling becomes more important to keep equipment working safely.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a thermometer icon and red heat waves, linked from the hardware box.

steps.label: Cooling and operations
steps.explanation: Cooling systems, buildings and networking add more resource use. Some sites use significant water for cooling, while others use less.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a fan, pipe and network icon. Add labels 'cooling', 'water', and 'network'.

steps.label: Environmental footprint
steps.explanation: The result can include energy use, water use, emissions and hardware impacts. Carbon footprint is one part of this wider picture.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box with four small labels: 'energy', 'water', 'emissions', 'materials/e-waste'. Use a bracket to show emissions are a subset of environmental footprint.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping a box highlights the next box to show the causal chain; a toggle switches the final label between 'narrow view: carbon only' and 'broader view: environmental footprint'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a five-step flow. First, an AI task starts the process, such as training a model or answering a prompt. Second, hardware like chips and servers performs calculations and uses electricity. Third, those calculations create heat. Fourth, cooling systems, networking and other operations use additional resources, and some facilities also use water for cooling. Fifth, the combined result is the environmental footprint: energy use, water use, greenhouse gas emissions, and hardware-related impacts such as material use and electronic waste. A note explains that carbon footprint is only one part of the broader environmental footprint.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right flow chart with five labelled boxes and arrows: AI task, hardware runs, heat builds up, cooling and operations, environmental footprint. A note under the final box says 'carbon footprint is one part of environmental footprint'.

workedExample.scenario: A small public information team compares two ways to group 12,000 short survey comments into themes.
workedExample.input: Option A uses a large hosted model for all comments. Option B first removes duplicates and very short entries, then uses a smaller model on 8,000 comments.
process: The team defines the same output for both options: 10 issue groups and short summaries.
They estimate the processing needed and note that Option A sends all 12,000 comments to a larger service, while Option B reduces the volume first.
They check operational information from their provider: the larger option uses more server time and the provider notes water-cooled facilities in some regions.
They choose Option B because it meets the quality need with less processing, fewer repeat runs and lower expected energy use.
workedExample.result: Both options produce usable topic groups, but the smaller, cleaner workflow avoids unnecessary processing. The team cannot claim an exact carbon number from this test alone, yet it can credibly say the second option likely has a lower overall footprint.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A humanitarian coordination team wants help grouping incoming non-sensitive field reports into common logistics issues so staff can spot repeated supply bottlenecks faster.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This is a case where AI may save staff time, but leaders still need to ask whether the chosen model, hosting setup and number of repeated runs are proportionate to the task and whether a simpler method would do.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not place confidential, personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or operationally sensitive field information into an unapproved public AI service. Use approved tools, minimise data, and keep human oversight over outputs and decisions.

whyItMatters: This affects budgets, procurement, risk and credibility. Choosing a model or hosting option without asking about energy, water and emissions can create avoidable cost and environmental impact. For leaders and policy staff, the key question is not 'AI or no AI' but 'what level of capability is needed, under what safeguards, and at what operational trade-off?' Clearer terms help organisations compare options, ask vendors better questions and avoid treating carbon alone as the whole story.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Carbon footprint, environmental footprint and sustainability all mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They overlap, but they are different scopes. Carbon footprint focuses on greenhouse gas emissions. Environmental footprint is broader and may include water, materials and electronic waste. Sustainability is broader again because it also asks whether the system remains workable and responsible over time, including operational trade-offs.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Only training a model matters; using it later has little impact.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Training can be very resource-intensive, but repeated everyday use can also add up, especially at large scale. A model serving millions of requests, generating long outputs or being called many times in a workflow can have substantial ongoing energy demand.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If two systems use the same amount of compute, they have the same environmental impact.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Compute is only part of the picture. Environmental impact also depends on hardware efficiency, how the data centre is cooled, where the electricity comes from, how much networking is involved and how long the hardware lasts. Similar processing work can therefore lead to different emissions or water use.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: AI needs real machines in real buildings. Those machines use electricity, create heat, and may need water for cooling. The wider environmental impact depends on how much processing is done and where and how the system is run.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: The footprint of an AI system arises across training and inference, plus storage, networking and facility overheads. Direct operational impacts include electricity consumed by processors and supporting infrastructure, and sometimes water used in cooling. Carbon footprint refers specifically to greenhouse gas emissions associated with that resource use and potentially other lifecycle stages, depending on the accounting boundary used. Environmental footprint is a broader category that can include energy demand, water consumption, embodied impacts in hardware manufacture, material extraction and end-of-life electronic waste. Sustainability is the wider judgement about whether a system delivers sufficient value relative to these impacts and other constraints over time. This is why boundary-setting matters: a comparison may count only model inference, or it may include training, idle capacity, transmission, cooling overhead and hardware lifecycle. The term is commonly confused with compute, but compute is a measure of processing work, not a full environmental outcome.

keyTakeaway: AI is digital on the surface but physical underneath, so better choices about models, hardware and deployment can reduce real-world resource use.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best shows the difference between these related terms?
options: Carbon footprint covers emissions only, while environmental footprint can also include water, materials and e-waste.
Environmental footprint means only electricity use, while sustainability means only carbon emissions.
Sustainability is just another word for model size.
Compute and environmental footprint are interchangeable because both measure processing.
quickCheck.explanation: Carbon footprint is the narrower term because it focuses on greenhouse gas emissions. Environmental footprint is broader, and sustainability is broader still because it asks whether the overall approach remains responsible and workable over time. Compute helps explain resource use, but it is not the same as environmental impact.

energy and water use of ai
contested: The broad idea is clear, but exact measurement methods and accounting boundaries are genuinely debated. Different assessments may include or exclude training, inference, cooling overhead, network traffic, hardware manufacture and end-of-life impacts, so published figures are not always directly comparable.
